rules.title: Landlords may charge only first month's rent, last month's rent, security deposit and lock fee up front (no application fees)
rules.requirement: Before a tenancy starts, a Massachusetts landlord may only require first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit and the cost of a new lock. Application, pet, cleaning, amenity and other up-front fees are not allowed. According to the source, this includes requiring the applicant to pay a third-party screening service.
rules.key_value: Only first, last, security deposit, lock change allowed; application fees prohibited for lessors
rules.coverage_conditions: All lessors of residential rental housing in Massachusetts.
rules.exemptions: Licensed real estate brokers may charge fees under separate rules (254 CMR 7).
rules.quoted_span: spells out the list of charges that landlords may ask tenants to pay at the start of a tenancy: first month’s rent, last month’s rent, security deposit, and lock-change fee.
rules.penalty: Damages; the source cites a federal court (Perry v. Equity Residential, 2014) that awarded triple damages and attorney's fees for unlawful application fees.

rules.title: Licensed broker fee disclosure requirements for prospective tenants
rules.requirement: Only a licensed broker may charge a prospective tenant a fee for finding an apartment. At the first personal meeting, the broker must tell you in writing the fee amount, when and how it is paid, and whether it depends on a lease being signed, and must ask you to sign that notice.
rules.key_value: Written fee disclosure at first personal meeting; broker must be licensed
rules.coverage_conditions: Real estate brokers and salespeople who deal with prospective tenants in Massachusetts.
rules.quoted_span: In addition to holding a valid license, the broker has to tell the applicant in writing the amount of the broker’s fee, the time and manner of payment, and whether it is contingent on the owner and applicant actually entering into a lease or rental agreement.
rules.conflict_note: This secondary source does not mention later changes to Massachusetts broker-fee law (for example, the 2025 shift that makes whoever hires the broker pay the fee). Check against the current statute before relying on it for who pays the broker fee.

notes: The source is a secondary page from a landlord association (MassLandlords), not official text. The article says the M.G.L. c. 186 § 15B rule on up-front charges has been in effect "since the 1970s" but gives no exact effective date, so effective_date is left null. Its views on tenant-paid third-party screening services, landlords who are also brokers, and rejected applicants are attorney opinion and non-binding court cases (Perry, Woodruff, Samia), not separate rules. The article does not address the 2025 Massachusetts broker-fee reform, so the broker-fee record may be out of date. The article does not discuss security deposit limits or interest rules beyond listing the deposit as an allowed charge, so no deposit rule was extracted.
